content: Tuberculosis (TB) prevention and control, as well as its diagnosis, are critical areas of focus in global health. HIV infections often complicate TB management, as HIV is the strongest risk factor for developing active TB disease in individuals with latent or new Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections. The risk of developing TB is approximately 30 times higher in people living with HIV compared to those without HIV. TB is responsible for over a quarter of deaths among individuals living with HIV. Isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) is a key intervention for preventing TB in people living with HIV. In 2011, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued guidelines recommending at least six months of IPT for children and adults living with HIV, including pregnant women, those receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), and those who have successfully completed TB treatment. Additionally, WHO conditionally recommended 36 months of IPT (as a proxy for lifelong or continuous treatment) for individuals living with HIV in settings with high TB prevalence and transmission. This recommendation was based on unpublished data at the time, with concerns about feasibility, adverse events, and the quality of evidence. Since then, new studies, including randomized controlled trials, have been published, prompting WHO to reassess the evidence and update the recommendation. The updated guidelines aim to evaluate the provision of 36 months of IPT for children and adults living with HIV, including pregnant women, those on ART, and those who have completed TB treatment, in high TB and HIV prevalence settings. The update is intended for healthcare workers, policymakers, program managers, governments, non-governmental organizations, donors, and patient support groups addressing HIV and TB in resource-constrained settings. The guideline development process involved a WHO Steering Group, a Guidelines Development Group (comprising external experts, national program managers, academics, and civil society representatives), and an External Review Group. The process adhered to WHO's recommended methodology, including systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses of outcomes of interest. The GRADE system was used to assess the quality of evidence and develop recommendations. The key question addressed was whether 36 months (or longer) of IPT, compared to six months, reduces the likelihood of progression to active TB in people living with HIV. Outcomes of interest included active TB incidence, confirmed TB, mortality, HIV disease progression, adverse events, and adherence. The quality of evidence was rated as low, and the conditionality of the recommendation was influenced by considerations of TB epidemiology, health infrastructure, programmatic priorities, and patient adherence. The guidelines aim to support healthcare providers and policymakers in implementing effective TB prevention strategies tailored to the needs of individuals and communities.
